questions.q: Name two active sensors and two passive sensors commonly used in Earth observation satellites, and state the primary energy source for each.
questions.a: Active sensors: Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) on Sentinel-1 (microwave pulses generated by the satellite), LiDAR on ICESat-2 (laser pulses generated by the satellite). Passive sensors: Multispectral Scanner (MSS) on Landsat (solar radiation reflected in visible/NIR), Thermal Infrared Sensor (TIRS) on Landsat (terrestrial thermal emission). A wrong answer—e.g., listing Landsat MSS as active—reveals the student thinks any satellite-borne instrument is “active” just because it is on a satellite, confusing platform with sensor energy source.

questions.q: Why can a C-band radar sensor (active) acquire usable images of the Brahmaputra floodplain at 2 am during a cloudy monsoon night, while a Landsat-8 OLI sensor (passive) cannot?
questions.a: The radar emits its own 5.6 cm microwave pulses, which penetrate cloud droplets and require no solar illumination; the backscattered signal is recorded regardless of time or weather. Landsat-8 OLI relies on solar radiation reflected in the visible/NIR bands—at night there is no sunlight, and thick monsoon clouds block/reflect the incoming solar energy before it reaches the surface. A wrong answer that says “radar uses sunlight too” shows the student has not grasped the self-illumination concept central to active sensing.

questions.q: You are tasked with mapping the extent of standing water in Punjab’s rice fields during the kharif season (July–September). Cloud cover is persistent. Which specific satellite sensor would you choose, and what are the two key technical reasons for your choice?
questions.a: Choose Sentinel-1 SAR (C-band, VV/VH polarisation). Reason 1: Active microwave at 5.6 cm penetrates cloud and rain, providing all-weather imaging. Reason 2: The revisit time of 6 days (with two satellites) allows frequent monitoring of rapid flood changes. A student who picks Landsat-8 because “it has better resolution” ignores the cloud constraint, showing inability to match sensor capability to environmental conditions.

questions.q: Compare the geometric distortions introduced by a whiskbroom scanner and a pushbroom scanner when imaging a mountainous region like the Western Ghats. Which scanner produces more reliable planimetric accuracy and why?
questions.a: A whiskbroom scanner uses a single detector per band with an oscillating mirror; the varying look angle across the swath causes panoramic distortion (pixels at the edge are stretched) and relief displacement that changes with scan angle. A pushbroom scanner uses a linear array of thousands of fixed detectors; each ground pixel is viewed at a constant nadir angle, so geometric distortion is uniform and easier to correct. Therefore, pushbroom scanners (e.g., on Cartosat-2, Sentinel-2) yield better planimetric accuracy in rugged terrain. A wrong answer claiming whiskbroom is better because “it has a mirror” confuses mechanical complexity with geometric fidelity.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: “For monitoring wheat crop health in the Indo-Gangetic Plain during the rabi season (November–March), a passive optical sensor like Sentinel-2 MSI is always superior to an active microwave sensor like Sentinel-1 SAR.” Provide two arguments for and one limitation of the statement.
questions.a: For: (1) Sentinel-2 provides 10 m resolution in red and NIR bands, enabling precise NDVI calculation for chlorophyll content; (2) its 5-day revisit (with two satellites) captures rapid phenological changes. Limitation: Rabi season can have fog/haze; optical data may be lost for weeks, while Sentinel-1 SAR penetrates haze and provides soil moisture and structural information complementary to NDVI. A student who says “optical is always better because it has more bands” fails to evaluate the temporal reliability trade-off in real Indian conditions.

questions.q: Design a two-sensor strategy to simultaneously map urban heat islands and impervious surface expansion in Bengaluru over a 5-year period. Specify the sensors, their types (active/passive), acquisition timing, and one key parameter each will measure.
questions.a: Sensor 1 (passive): Landsat-8/9 TIRS (Thermal Infrared Sensor) – acquire night-time (10:30 pm) images in pre-monsoon (April) to measure land-surface temperature (LST) for heat island intensity. Sensor 2 (passive): Sentinel-2 MSI – acquire cloud-free day-time images in the same season to calculate Normalised Difference Built-up Index (NDBI) for impervious surface extent. Both are passive optical/thermal; active radar is not needed here because clouds are minimal in April and the parameters (LST, NDBI) are best derived from optical/thermal bands. A poor answer selects radar for heat islands, misunderstanding that LST requires thermal infrared emission, not microwave backscatter.
